title: The stochastic multi-gradient algorithm for multi-objective optimization and its application to supervised machine learning
contribution: Shows that the stochastic multi-gradient direction (a min-norm convex combination of sampled gradients) is biased even when the individual gradients are unbiased. Under a bias bound proportional to the step size it proves SG-like rates for a weighted gap: O(1/k) under strong convexity and O(1/sqrt(k)) under convexity. It wraps SMG in a list-based Pareto-front algorithm (PF-SMG), tested on 13 noisy DMS problems and on fairness in logistic classification. Read from arXiv v3 (Feb 2021).
problem_entry: A gap where two mature methods meet: SG is well understood and deterministic multi-gradient descent is well understood, but 'little is known yet about stochastic multi-gradient descent'. The predecessor [43] missed the bias property and needed 'strong and unnatural assumptions', and it had no Pareto-front version (p. 5).
key_idea: Feed sampled gradients into the same dual QP as the deterministic multi-gradient method and step as in projected SG (Algorithm 1, p. 8). The QP acts as a nonlinear map, so the output is biased (p. 9). Tolerate a bias of order alpha_k, enforced by growing batch sizes (pp. 6, 17). Build the front by list updates: perturb at the largest holes, run SMG several times, drop dominated points (Algorithm 2, pp. 18-19).
assumptions: Lipschitz gradients (5.1). Unbiased individual gradients, a first-moment error bound proportional to alpha_k, and a variance bound (5.2). Bounded X with diameter Theta (5.3). A globally Lipschitz QP solution map, admitted to be only locally justified (5.4, p. 12). Strong convexity (5.5) or convexity (5.7). The stronger 5.6 (lambda_k 'identifies well' lambda*) is needed for the rate against the limit (pp. 10-16). Random variables independent across objectives (p. 5). The synthetic experiments violate unbiasedness, as stated on p. 22.
proof_devices: classical SG distance recursion E||x_{k+1}-x*||^2 with a nonexpansive projection (Nemirovski et al. template) (p. 14)
null-term insertion splitting the cross term into ideal term + multi-gradient bias + weight perturbation (eq. (22), p. 14)
bias bounded by alpha_k L_gradS via Jensen and Assumption 5.2(b); multiplied by the domain diameter Theta, it becomes order alpha_k^2 (pp. 11-12, 14)
weight perturbation bounded via the Lipschitz QP solution map (constant beta) and linearity of grad_x S in lambda: alpha_k beta L_gradS M_S (p. 13)
weighted telescoping with alpha_k = 2/(c(k+1)) and weights s, giving a gap against averaged weights lambda_bar_k = sum s lambda_s / sum s; sign caveat stated (pp. 13-15)
extra assumption 5.6 giving the contraction (1 - 2 alpha_k c) and the induction of [38, Eqs. (2.9)-(2.10)] for E||x_k - x*||^2 = O(1/k) (pp. 15-16)
convex case: alpha_k = alpha_bar/sqrt(k) with Theta^2 telescoping and a simple-average lambda_bar_k (Appendix A, pp. 26-27)
batch-size realization of the bias bound: Var of batch mean <= sigma^2/b and E||X|| <= sigma sqrt(n) for Gaussian X (p. 17)
experiments: Monte Carlo bias exhibit (n = 4, m = 2, N = 3000, 10^4 batches per batch size; pp. 9-10). Fairness on 4 LIBSVM sets split by a binary feature, with per-group logistic losses (pp. 19-22). 13 DMS-collection problems with uniform noise on the variables (p. 22). Same 30 starts; new points per iteration equalized (PF-SMG p = 2, r = 5 vs PF-MG p = 1, r = 10); the run with average Gamma out of 10 is reported. Purity, Gamma and Delta shown as profiles and in Table 4. Losses are reported: lower purity, e.g. FF1 0.630 vs 0.982. Costs are counted in iterations and CPU only. The only baseline is the authors' own deterministic PF-MG. The PF-SMG batch size is not stated, and there is no code statement (pp. 18-25).
positioning: Extends Robbins-Monro SG and the Fliege-Svaiter multi-gradient method, with the deterministic rates of Fliege-Vaz-Vicente [25]. Direct critique of predecessor [43], including a footnote comparing assumptions. NSGA-II/AMOSA are criticized for having no theory and being slow, and a priori scalarization for three drawbacks. Self-citations are DMS [13] (method, list update, test set, Delta metric), [25] and the fairness report [36], 3 of 52 references (pp. 2-5, 15, 18-19, 22, 28-30).
writing: Survey-style introduction, then a modest contribution sentence ('providing an understanding of the behavior and basic properties'). A separate phenomenon section (intuition figure + Monte Carlo bias plot) comes before the theory. Each theorem is followed by an interpretation with explicit caveats ('Rigorously speaking … not even guaranteed to be positive'). Minor typos survive in v3 (pp. 4-6, 9-10, 15, 24).
limits_future: Stated limits: no stopping criterion, a stronger assumption for the rate against lambda*, possible negative gap, slower weight averaging in the convex case, lower purity of PF-SMG, and biased gradients in the synthetic tests. Not stated: no front theory, no sample-complexity count, only a self-baseline. Future: noise/variance reduction, non-box feasible regions, proximal terms for nonsmooth regularizers, deep learning, nonconvex rates (pp. 8, 15-16, 22-26).

method_links.note: The SG skeleton is kept. The changed object is the direction subproblem's input (sampled instead of true gradients), not an acceptance test, since SG has none. Steps 5 and 6 are evidenced: the price (bias) is stated in the abstract, and class-native metrics Purity, Gamma, Delta are used.

The rates are placed next to SG's ('of order similar to what is known for stochastic gradient'). Variant aspects: the unit is iterations, with no sample count despite growing batches, no lower-bound question, and the gap is measured with averaged weights as in S015.

An accuracy requirement tied to the step size (first-moment gradient error <= alpha_k(...)) is realized by dynamic batch growth. It is an expectation condition, not a probability-p condition, and has no threshold.

Reuses 13 DMS-collection problems, performance profiles and class-native metrics, with a real application and visible losses. But the only baseline is the authors' own deterministic counterpart, and the text has no code statement (code is in the companion S016).
Reversed structure, as in S016: a heuristic outer list loop (perturb at the largest holes, p restarts, filter) around SMG trajectories that carry guarantees. There is no theorem for the front.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Unbiased gradient estimates pass through the nonlinear QP solution map, so the output is biased. The bias is shown by a Monte Carlo plot, then tolerated at O(alpha_k) and enforced by batch growth.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: averaged-weight gap with a two-tier theorem
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A weak rate against the iterates' averaged weights, with a stated sign caveat, then a strong rate against lambda* under one named extra assumption. The same device appears in S015 (c05), so 2 papers.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: diagnose the predecessor's strong assumption as a symptom of a missed property
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: [43] 'failed to identify a critical property' and so needed 'strong and unnatural assumptions'. A footnote shows that its key inequality would follow from the authors' own condition if the direction were unbiased.
This is the theory half, with a first fairness demonstration. It forwards the detailed accuracy-fairness study to [36] (S016).

transferable: Null-term three-way split of the SG cross term (ideal + estimator bias + weight perturbation). Make each error O(alpha_k) and multiply by the domain diameter so it matches the alpha_k^2 variance term (pp. 13-14).

When the algorithm cannot know its limiting target, prove a rate against the iterates' averaged target and flag the sign issue. Then add one named assumption for the rate against the limit (pp. 13-16).
State a new noise assumption in step-size units (error <= alpha_k * const) and show a batch-size rule that enforces it (pp. 11, 17).
Before the theory, exhibit a suspected estimator bias with a Monte Carlo plot of ||E[estimator - target]|| against batch size (10^4 replications) (pp. 9-10).
When comparing list-based Pareto-front methods, equalize the new points added per iteration, and add points only at the largest gap along each objective axis (p. 19).
Footnote a line-by-line comparison of your assumption with the predecessor's stronger one (p. 15).

quotes.text: it is shown that this direction is biased even when all individual gradient estimators are unbiased.

The authors in [43] introduced and analyzed it, but failed to identify a critical property about the stochastic multi-gradient direction, and as a consequence analyzed the method under strong and unnatural assumptions.
